questions.prompt: With about 100 redirects for every link created, which part of the design matters most for performance?

options.text: Making link creation as fast as possible
Serving redirects from a cache, because reads dominate

questions.explanation: Reads outnumber writes 100 to 1, and a few links get most clicks, so caching redirects removes most of the load.

questions.prompt: Why does the design return 302 rather than 301 for redirects?

options.text: Browsers cache 301s, so later clicks skip our servers, breaking click counts and link expiry
301 is not allowed for external URLs

questions.explanation: A permanent redirect is remembered by browsers. That saves load but means we stop seeing clicks and can't expire or take down a link for people who already followed it.

questions.prompt: Why use 7 base62 characters for 6 billion random codes, when 6 characters give 57 billion?

options.text: With 6 characters the space would be over 10% full, so random codes would collide often; 7 characters keep it under 0.2% full

questions.explanation: Random generation needs plenty of spare space: the collision rate equals the fraction of codes already used.

questions.prompt: What are the problems with a single global counter encoded in base62?

options.text: It is a bottleneck and a single point of failure
Sequential codes let anyone enumerate every link
It needs coordination on every link creation

questions.explanation: A counter never collides, but one shared counter needs coordination per write and makes codes guessable. Handing out ranges and scrambling numbers fixes most of that.

questions.prompt: The cache cluster fails during peak traffic with a 95% hit rate. Roughly how much does read load on the store increase?
questions.explanation: With a 95% hit rate the store serves 5% of reads. Without the cache it serves 100%: twenty times as much. Size the store, or protect it, for that case.
